title: Tenant dependency graph and deferred-upgrade canvas
creator: Avery Chen
description: Design a combined visualization and interaction surface for Private/VPC tenants that 1) renders a tenant-level dependency graph showing cluster, control plane, and service connectivity within the VPC (including cross-region links) and 2) surfaces a deferred-upgrade canvas where operators can schedule, annotate, and simulate upgrade windows with rollback playbook steps. The goal is to reduce upgrade blast radius, accelerate incident triage by surfacing likely affected downstream services, and make delayed upgrades explicit and auditable in the Console.
background: Customer engineering teams running Redwood Private ask for clearer impact visibility when scheduling control-plane or runtime upgrades. Current upgrade UI hides downstream service relationships and requires opening multiple consoles and runbooks. This proposal merges a read-only dependency visualization with an interactive upgrade staging area so operators can see real connectivity and pre-author rollbacks before triggering windows.
acceptance_criteria: Graph renders tenant resources (clusters, gateways, endpoints) with edge latency and egress cost metadata visible on hover
Operators can create a deferred upgrade in the canvas and attach a rollback playbook with step templates
Simulate button produces a deterministic list of potentially affected services and an estimated impact score
Audit log entry is created for scheduled upgrades with author, description, and linked rollback playbook
Design passes accessibility review (keyboard nav + screen reader labels)
prototype_notes: Initial layout uses force-directed graph with cluster-as-node grouping and an expandable pane for node metadata
Canvas supports drag-to-link for manual dependency adjustments (temporary local annotations) that persist to a per-tenant draft
Simulate uses a heuristics engine: 1) immediate neighbors, 2) tentatively affected by KV cache hotpaths, 3) cross-region latency-sensitive services flagged
Collapsed-mode tile provides a one-line summary for tenants with high service counts
tradeoffs_and_risks: Force-directed graphs can be noisy for tenants with >200 resources; we propose progressive disclosure and sampling
Simulate accuracy depends on runtime topology import frequency; stale topology can misrepresent risk
Adding heavy interactivity may impact Console frontend performance; plan to lazy-load graph worker and memoize layout results
open_questions: Should we allow edits on the dependency graph to persist to the canonical topology source, or only local annotations?
What are guardrails for automated rollback triggers versus manual execution?
What RBAC scope should control who can create deferred upgrades versus who can only comment?
decisions: Prefer non-invasive approach: graph edits are local annotations by default; separate Issue/PR workflow required to push structural topology changes
Rollback playbooks should support templated steps and an optional dry-run mode; automatic trigger will be gated behind a separate feature flag and audit trail
implementation_notes: Frontend: React + WebGL canvas for heavy graphs, worker thread for layout; lazy-load on first open
Backend: expose tenant-topology snapshot API endpoint with versioning; simulate endpoint returns list of affected resource IDs and an impact score
Telemetry: track simulate runs, scheduled upgrades created, and playbook attachments for future cost and reliability analysis
